body: Decide from your own setup

| Your situation | Likely fit | Check |
|---|---|---|
| You have a usable counter or kitchen worktop, fridge space and water | A bartender | Who brings tools, glassware and ice |
| You have the space but no bar or equipment | Staff plus equipment, or a staffed mobile bar | What the bar needs: floor space, access, power if the supplier specifies it |
| You want one team to handle everything | A full bar package | What the package includes and excludes |
| You want to supply your own drinks | A bartender, or a supplier that offers it | Venue rules and supplier terms: see [supplying your own alcohol](/stories/supply-own-alcohol-hire-bartender) |
Why suppliers describe things differently

Some suppliers publish separate staff-only, staffed-bar and stocked-package options, and others quote around your brief. Terms such as "dry hire" are used in different ways, so read the inclusions rather than the label. See [dry bar hire explained](/stories/dry-bar-hire-staffed-bar-full-bar-service).
When one specialist operator makes sense

A direct mobile bar company can suit a host who wants a single point of contact and a complete, tailored service. A booking platform can suit a host who wants to choose a person and see exactly what is paid for. Neither is better in every case.

choose-a-signature-cocktail-for-your-par.title: A Signature Cocktail for the Whole Party
choose-a-signature-cocktail-for-your-par.seo: Choose a signature cocktail for your party
choose-a-signature-cocktail-for-your-par.alt: A creamy layered cocktail topped with dried raspberry and herbs, on a black saucer with a spoon.
choose-a-signature-cocktail-for-your-par.blurb: One well-chosen drink gives the party its theme. Here is how to choose it and brief your bartender.
choose-a-signature-cocktail-for-your-par.intro: Pick one drink that matches your occasion and that a bartender can make quickly in volume. That single choice becomes the party's signature, and it makes the rest of the planning easier.
body: Start with the occasion

Think about what the party is celebrating, the season and the mood. A summer garden party calls for something fresh and long. An autumn dinner suits something warm and rounded. A drink that fits the moment feels intentional to guests.
Add a flavour your group already loves
If your guests enjoy citrus, berries, coffee or ginger, begin there. A familiar flavour in a new combination feels special without being unfamiliar.
Make it easy to serve

A signature drink works best when it can be prepared the same way many times. Tell the bartender how many guests you expect and when drinks begin, and they can advise on whether a recipe suits the pace of your evening. For quantities, see [how many cocktails to plan for your guests](/stories/how-many-cocktails-for-a-party).
Offer an alcohol-free match

Many hosts like a matching alcohol-free version of the signature drink, so everyone shares in the theme. Another option is a separate alcohol-free drink with its own flavour. Choose the one that suits your guests.
A simple brief

This example is illustrative:

| Brief item | Example |
|---|---|
| Occasion | A summer birthday in the garden |
| Flavour | Citrus and mint |
| Timing | Served as guests arrive, then through the first hour |
| Servings | Guest numbers shared with the bartender in advance |
| Alcohol-free | A matching version with the same garnish |
A note on recipes

If you book a bar company, their signature recipes may belong to them. The company decides which recipes it makes available, so ask what is on offer. To build a menu around several drinks, read [how to plan a cocktail menu for a party](/stories/how-to-plan-a-cocktail-menu-for-a-party).

cocktail-party-ice-and-glassware.alt: Rows of foamy coupe cocktails with cherries at an event bar.
cocktail-party-ice-and-glassware.blurb: Plan ice separately for serving and for chilling, and plan glassware around how many glasses are in use at once and how quickly they come back. Your bartender or bar company can confirm...
cocktail-party-ice-and-glassware.intro: Plan ice separately for serving and for chilling, and plan glassware around how many glasses are in use at once and how quickly they come back. Your bartender or bar company can confirm the numbers for your menu. The figures below are planning examples with their assumptions shown.
body: Ice

- **Serving ice** goes into drinks, so it depends on how many cocktails and how many are served over ice.
- **Chilling ice** keeps bottles and mixers cold. Use a separate tub.
- **Storage.** Ice melts fast, so check freezer space and delivery time.
Glassware

- **Types.** A short glass, a tall glass and one stemmed glass cover most menus.
- **Quantity.** Plan enough for most guests to have a glass in hand, plus spares for ones in use or being washed.
- **Reuse.** If glasses are collected and washed, you need fewer. If they are not, you need many more.
- **Alternatives.** Check the venue for restrictions on glass outdoors.
Who provides it

It depends on the package. A bartender alone may not bring ice or glassware, while a bar company usually provides stock, glassware, ice and the bar. Use the [responsibility checklist](/stories/what-to-provide-when-hiring-a-bartender).
Ask your supplier

1. How much ice will my menu need, and who is bringing it?
2. How many glasses are included, and are they collected and washed?
3. What happens to leftovers?

cocktail-party-timeline.title: What to Put in a Cocktail Party Timeline
cocktail-party-timeline.seo: What to put in a cocktail party timeline
cocktail-party-timeline.alt: A creamy iced coffee cocktail with a straw, close up.
cocktail-party-timeline.blurb: A sample timeline and a short checklist to agree with your bartender before the party.
cocktail-party-timeline.intro: A good timeline names six moments: access and setup, guest arrival, the first round, a toast or food, last orders and pack-down. Agree them with your bartender and the evening runs on a plan you both know.
body: An example timeline

These times are an example. Adjust them for your own party.

| Time | Moment | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| 17:00 | Access and setup | The bartender arrives, meets you and sets up the bar |
| 18:30 | Guest arrival | Doors open and the bar is ready |
| 18:45 | First round | Welcome drinks go out |
| 20:00 | Toast or food | A toast, or dinner begins, with service paused or slowed |
| 22:00 | Last orders | The bartender announces the final round |
| 22:30 | Pack-down | The bar is cleared and the bartender finishes |
Agree these with your bartender

- **Who meets them** and where they arrive.
- **Where the bar goes**, including access to water, power and ice.
- **When the final headcount or menu is due**, if that applies to your service.
- **How the evening ends**, including the last-order moment.
Talk to the bartender directly

Alex Gagnon, founder of FireFlair, believes it works best when the bartender and the host communicate directly about the plan. A short conversation before the day answers most questions and means the bartender knows your party before they walk in.
Match the timeline to your format

If you chose a welcome-drinks start, a cocktail hour or a bar all evening, put that window at the top of the timeline. [Welcome drinks, a cocktail hour or a bar all evening](/stories/when-to-serve-cocktails-at-a-party) covers the choice. Then pick your signature drink with [a signature cocktail for the whole party](/stories/choose-a-signature-cocktail-for-your-party).
A checklist to send

Copy this into a message to your bartender:

1. Date, start and finish times.
2. Address and where to arrive.
3. Number of guests and how they arrive.
4. Menu and any alcohol-free drinks.
5. Who will meet you.

Browse FireFlair Packages to find the bar service that suits your plan. [How to book a bartender on FF Party](/stories/how-to-book-a-bartender-on-ff-party) shows the steps.

ff-party-booking-deposits-and-refunds.intro: To book on FF Party you pay a £50 deposit for your event. If we cannot find the staff for your event, the deposit is refunded in full. If your plans change, you can move your event date up to 30 days before it takes place, and your deposit goes with it.
body: What the deposit is

The £50 deposit secures your booking request and starts the search for your people. It is one deposit for the whole event, however many bartenders or other professionals you ask for. It is separate from the professionals' pay, which you see on its own line, and from the cost of drinks, equipment and travel.
When it is refunded

- **We cannot get the staff for your event.** The deposit is refunded in full.
- **You cancel before anyone is confirmed.** Use "Cancel request & refund".
- **You cancel at least 30 days before your event.** The deposit is refunded.
- **Only part of your event is staffed.** We look at it with you and decide individually.
- **Your bartender cancels.** We reopen the position and look for a replacement, with no second matching fee. Replacements depend on availability.
Not sure of the date?
You can book now and change the date later, as long as it is at least 30 days before the event. Your deposit stays with your booking.
Once your team is confirmed

When your staff are confirmed, they hold your date. If you cancel within 30 days of the event after that, the deposit is not refunded, which protects the professionals who have kept the date free for you. If you cancel earlier than that, at least 30 days before the event, your deposit is refunded.
Where is the record?

Your booking page on the website is the official record. WhatsApp and email carry notifications.

golden-age-of-parties.blurb: What research on live experiences and smaller gatherings could mean for the way we celebrate with friends and family.
golden-age-of-parties.intro: Think of the birthday dinner where everyone stays for one more drink, or the evening a friend learns to make their favourite cocktail. These are the kinds of moments you have to be there for. At FireFlair, we think the next wave of parties could start with more people making time for evenings like these. "Golden age" is our view, not a proven fact: the research below shows the appetite, and you can decide what it means for your next celebration.
body: Why getting together matters

The World Health Organization estimates that about one in six people worldwide, or 15.8%, report feeling lonely. That gives some context for why social connection deserves attention. Source: [World Health Organization, Social connection](https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/social-connection).

In July 2025, Eventbrite's research partner dcdx surveyed 4,051 people aged 18–35 in the US and UK. In the survey, 79% expected to attend more events in 2026, rising to 82% among UK respondents. A separate US study by Archrival found that 74% of Gen Z respondents put more value on in-person experiences than digital ones. Sources: [Eventbrite Social Study 2026, pp. 4 and 25](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260114088488/en); Archrival research reported by Vogue Business.
What smaller gatherings can offer

Eventbrite reported that attendance at micro-events on its platform rose 23% in 2024. For a host, the appeal of a smaller gathering can be personal. There is room to choose a drink for the birthday guest, bring friends into the kitchen, and give everyone a chance to try their hand at making a cocktail. Source: [Eventbrite TRNDS 2025, p. 14](https://www.eventbrite.com/blog/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Eventbrite-TRNDS-2025-UKI.pdf).
The people who make it happen

Grand View Research estimates that the global event management market was worth US$1.16 trillion in 2024 and projects it could reach US$2.09 trillion by 2033. That estimate spans conferences, weddings, social events, sport, and live entertainment. A private celebration is one part of that much wider market. Source: [Grand View Research, Event Management Market](https://www.grandviewresearch.com/industry-analysis/event-management-market-report).

At home, a bartender can keep drinks moving while the host catches up with friends. At a bigger celebration, DJs, caterers, planners, and venues can all play a part. Pick an occasion you'd love to celebrate and give the people you want there a date to put in the diary.

how-many-bartenders-do-i-need.intro: A planning guide, not a rule. As a general recommendation: for up to 30 guests, one experienced bartender; for 30 to 100 guests, an experienced bartender plus support staff; for 100 or more, a team of bartenders, and we usually suggest a bar company that can supply the stock, glassware, ice and bar if you want them.
body: What pushes the number up

- **A cocktail menu** takes longer per drink than beer, wine or a short list of simple mixed drinks.
- **A peak.** Guests arriving together, or a toast, create a queue that a quiet evening does not.
- **Short service windows.** A two-hour welcome drinks service is busier than a five-hour party.
- **No support.** A bartender who also fetches ice and clears glasses serves fewer drinks.
- **Layout.** Two service points halve the walking but need two people.
The three sizes

| Guests | What we recommend | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Up to 30 | One experienced bartender | A steady house party with a short cocktail list is comfortably served by one person |
| 30 to 100 | An experienced bartender plus support staff | Support staff keep ice, glasses and restocking moving, so the bartender can keep serving |
| 100 or more | A team of bartenders, usually through a bar company | A bar company can provide the bar, stock, glassware and ice at your request, and run the whole service |

These are planning estimates for a conversation with the bartender or bar company, and they change with your menu, arrival pattern and venue.
How to plan it

1. Choose the drinks you will offer. See [how to plan a cocktail menu](/stories/how-to-plan-a-cocktail-menu-for-a-party).
2. Decide the busiest hour and how many guests will want a drink in it.
3. Decide who helps with ice and glasses.
4. Request the positions you need on your Event Card. Each position is invited and confirmed separately.

For a corporate event, see [staffing a product launch or drinks reception](https://ffstaff.uk/stories/staffing-a-product-launch-or-drinks-reception).

how-many-cocktails-for-a-party.alt: A long line of pink cocktails with cherries under purple party lights.
how-many-cocktails-for-a-party.blurb: Estimate servings by thinking about how long the bar is open, how many guests will want a cocktail, and how many other drinks are available. These are planning figures to discuss with...
how-many-cocktails-for-a-party.intro: Estimate servings by thinking about how long the bar is open, how many guests will want a cocktail, and how many other drinks are available. These are planning figures to discuss with your bartender, not rules about how much anyone should drink.
body: The method

1. **Guests who will want a cocktail.** Not everyone will, particularly if there is wine, beer or soft drinks.
2. **Hours of service.** Most guests have a first drink quickly, then pace themselves.
3. **Alcohol-free servings.** Include mocktails as real servings: some guests will not drink alcohol.
4. **Spread across drinks.** Divide the servings across your menu. Three cocktails and two alcohol-free drinks is a good starting point, and the choice is yours.
Worked example (illustrative)

A 40-guest party with the bar open for four hours. Say about 30 guests want cocktails, averaging 3 each: that is 90 servings. Add some extra for alcohol-free guests and busy moments and plan around 100 servings.

On FF Party, quantities are set in servings, in steps of 20. In this example you would choose 100 servings, spread across your chosen drinks. Your bartender can talk the numbers through with you.
Things that change the number

- A longer party, but quieter pacing.
- Other drinks on offer, such as wine or beer.
- A toast, which means everyone wants a drink at once.
- The weather, since hot days mean more soft and long drinks.

body: What changes the total

- **Hours of service**, including setup and clearing, not only the time guests are drinking.
- **Number of staff.** A larger or busier party needs more than one person. See [how many bartenders you need](/stories/how-many-bartenders-do-i-need).
- **Skills.** Classic cocktails, flair and a plain bar service are different jobs.
- **Equipment**, such as a bar, tools, glassware and ice.
- **Ingredients and alcohol**, and who supplies them.
- **Travel, delivery and parking.**
- **Minimum spend or minimum hours.**
- **VAT**, where the supplier charges it.
Ask every supplier the same questions

1. Is this the person only, the person with equipment, or a full package?
2. Are ingredients, ice and glassware included?
3. What is the minimum booking, and does travel cost extra?
4. Is VAT included in the price I am shown?
5. How is my booking confirmed, and what happens if the bartender cannot attend?

The [supplies checklist](/stories/what-to-provide-when-hiring-a-bartender) turns this into a list for your own venue.

|---|---|---|
| Poptop, London bartender listings | "From £120 per event"; individual listings from £210 and £270 per event | Platform listings for bartenders in London; the final price depends on guests, hours and menu |
| Poptop, UK cocktail bars | £33 per guest for all-inclusive drinks packages; around £325 per event for dry-hire cash bars (platform-reported averages) | Cocktail bar suppliers on the platform |
| BarOpsCo, London | £160 for bartender hire up to 3 hours; £300 for a cocktail bartender with setup up to 4 hours | One supplier's price guide; alcohol supplied by client or supplier |
| The Sesh Bars, London | Dry hire from £350; all-inclusive £6.50 to £7.50 per person per hour, excluding VAT | Bar, bartenders and glassware for dry hire; travel included inside the M25 |
| Mix & Twist, 2026 guide | £20 to £90 per head for mobile bars, standard service £20 to £50 | A mobile bar company's rough guide across styles |

Poptop's pages also show platform-wide averages that differ greatly between pages, so they are not used here. Check each supplier's current page, VAT and minimums before relying on any figure.

body: What you need before you start
Your phone number and email, the date, place, start and finish times, guest numbers, and the kind of night you want. You do not need an account for a company.
The steps

1. **Describe the event.** Occasion, guests, hours and location. It is saved as your Event Card.
2. **Choose your service.** A bartender, a cocktail bar service, a masterclass, a flair performance, or a team for a bigger night.
3. **Pay the £50 deposit.** It secures your request and is fully refunded if we cannot find the staff for your event.
4. **Choose your people.** Invite a bartender you like by name, or let Autofill invite professionals who match.
5. **Confirm.** See below.
What happens next

**Invited by name.** The bartender has up to 24 hours to reply, and never beyond the start of the event. If they accept, you are booked, with no second approval from you. The invitation is exclusive for your event; it does not reserve their whole diary.

**Autofill.** Invitations go to a batch of matching professionals, normally ten. "Available" is a reply, not a booking: you then pick the person you want. Choosing "Discuss first" does not confirm anything and does not extend any deadline. Each invitation has its own deadline, normally the earlier of seven days after it was created and the start of the event.
Does 24 hours mean I get an answer in 24 hours?
No. It is the time a professional has to reply. It is not a promise of a reply or of a confirmed booking within a day. If your date is close, say so in your request.
Want a bar company for a bigger night?
For larger events, the FireFlair team can contact bar companies for you. See [how to compare mobile bar companies](/stories/how-to-compare-mobile-bar-companies).
After you are confirmed

You both receive the booking details and the supported contact information. Your booking page on the website is the official record, and WhatsApp and email carry notifications. You can leave a review on the website after the event.
If your plans change

You can change your event date up to 30 days before. If a confirmed bartender cancels, we reopen the position and look for a replacement with no extra matching fee. See [how the deposit and refunds work](/stories/ff-party-booking-deposits-and-refunds).

body: Pick a bar spot

- A counter or table at least a metre and a half wide, away from the main walkway.
- Close to a fridge, a freezer, water and a place to wash up.
- Not in a doorway or the only route to the toilet.
Questions to settle with your bartender

1. **Access.** Where do they park and how do they carry things in?
2. **Setup time.** Bartenders usually arrive before guests so the bar is ready.
3. **Supplies.** Who brings alcohol, ingredients, ice and glassware? See [what to provide](/stories/what-to-provide-when-hiring-a-bartender).
4. **Menu.** Three cocktails and two alcohol-free drinks is a good starting point, and it is your choice. See [planning a cocktail menu](/stories/how-to-plan-a-cocktail-menu-for-a-party).
5. **Finish.** When service stops and who clears glasses.
Garden parties
Agree the ground and any shelter with the bartender beforehand, because a table on soft grass or in full sun needs thought. Ask about a plan B for rain, and where glasses will be collected.
Birthdays at home

A birthday usually has a toast or a cake moment when everyone wants a drink at once. Tell your bartender the time, so they are ready. For the number of people you need, see [how many bartenders you need](/stories/how-many-bartenders-do-i-need).

Travel and timing

Mobile bar companies often set an area they cover, and may add a travel charge beyond it. Ask where they travel from and how long they need to set up. Allow for traffic on the M25, A1(M) and M1 if your supplier is coming from outside the county.
Book early for popular dates

Questions to ask any supplier

- Do you cover my postcode, and is travel included?
- What do you bring, and what must I provide? See [what to provide](/stories/what-to-provide-when-hiring-a-bartender).
- How many bartenders do I need for my guest numbers? See [how many bartenders](/stories/how-many-bartenders-do-i-need).

In London the hard part is often logistics, not finding a bartender. Access, parking, lifts and venue rules can decide whether a cocktail service runs smoothly.
body: Logistics to settle early

- **Access.** Can equipment, ice and stock be brought in easily? A fourth-floor flat with no lift changes what a bartender can bring.
- **Parking and loading.** Ask your supplier whether they need a bay or a permit near the venue.
- **Space.** A cocktail bar needs a clear surface, water nearby and room to work.
- **Timing.** Venue curfews and neighbours affect setup and finish times.
Equipment and ice

Choosing the menu

how-to-host-a-cocktail-party-at-home.title: How to Host a Cocktail Party at Home
how-to-host-a-cocktail-party-at-home.seo: How to host a cocktail party at home
how-to-host-a-cocktail-party-at-home.alt: Two chilled martini glasses beside a cut-glass mixing glass full of ice on a wooden table.
how-to-host-a-cocktail-party-at-home.blurb: Plan the drinks, bar setup and timing for a cocktail party at home, with time to enjoy the evening with your guests.
how-to-host-a-cocktail-party-at-home.intro: To host a cocktail party at home, choose a short drinks menu, set up one place to serve it, and plan when you want the first round ready. Start with the moment you want everyone to share. For a birthday, that might be the first toast. For dinner with friends, it could be cocktails before you sit down. If you want the drinks to be the activity, make a cocktail masterclass part of the evening and give it a start time.
body: Choose a short drinks menu

Pick two or three drinks that suit the occasion. You could offer something bright and citrusy, a favourite of the guest of honour, and an alcohol-free option with its own garnish. A short menu gives each drink a place in the evening and makes the shopping list easier to work out. Agree the menu and who's supplying the ingredients before you shop.
Give the bar a place of its own

Choose a counter or table guests can approach while leaving space for others to move past. Think about where glassware, ice, and spare stock will go, and where guests can help themselves to water. If you're bringing in a bartender, share a photo of the space and agree when they can arrive to set up. Tell them how many guests you expect and when most people are likely to arrive.
Make time for the party itself

A bartender can prepare and serve the drinks while you greet your guests. A masterclass gives the group a shared activity, with someone to guide each round. Choose the format that fits the evening, then put the drinks, food, and any toast on a simple timeline. When the first drinks are ready, make sure you're there to raise a glass too.

Choose the FF Party experiences you are happy to put your name to. A private mixologist and a cocktail masterclass suit most properties. Each one carries its own duration and inclusions, so guests know what to expect before they book.
Tell guests what to expect before they arrive

Put the guest link in your pre-arrival guide, so the experience can be planned before the stay begins. Share the things guests ask most: how many people the space suits, whether visitors can join, when the evening needs to finish, and whether there is room to set up a bar.
Ask about guest preferences

Plan the handover

Agree who supplies the drinks, ice and glassware, and write it in your property answers so the professional and the guest see the same thing. Keep the exact address and access instructions in your private details. They are shared only with the people working at the property.
Work with local suppliers

how-to-plan-a-cocktail-menu-for-a-party.title: How to plan a cocktail menu for a party
how-to-plan-a-cocktail-menu-for-a-party.seo: How to plan a cocktail menu for a party
how-to-plan-a-cocktail-menu-for-a-party.blurb: Pick a short list that covers the main tastes, keeps the bartender's work manageable and includes good alcohol-free choices. Three cocktails and two alcohol-free drinks is a good...
how-to-plan-a-cocktail-menu-for-a-party.intro: Pick a short list that covers the main tastes, keeps the bartender's work manageable and includes good alcohol-free choices. Three cocktails and two alcohol-free drinks is a good starting point, but the menu is up to you. Your FF Party booking handles up to ten cocktails, with recipes provided, and a larger menu is usually a job for a bar company. More choice slows service for everyone.
body: A balanced list

- **One long, refreshing drink** that works as the default, such as a highball or spritz style.
- **One classic with a spirit-led flavour**, for guests who like a stronger drink.
- **One sweeter or fruitier option.**
- **One bitter or dry option**, if your guests will enjoy it.
- **At least one alcohol-free cocktail**, treated as a drink and not an afterthought.
Keep the service realistic

Drinks that are shaken, stirred or built over ice each take different amounts of time, and the more elaborate drinks slow a queue. If you expect a rush, keep most of the menu to quick builds and offer one or two showpiece drinks. This is also why [the number of bartenders](/stories/how-many-bartenders-do-i-need) depends on the menu.
Who supplies what

Decide with your supplier whether they bring the ingredients, you do, or the cost is shared. See [what to provide when you hire a bartender](/stories/what-to-provide-when-hiring-a-bartender) and [supplying your own alcohol](/stories/supply-own-alcohol-hire-bartender).
Using the FF Party menu

The FF Party cocktail menu opens with the UK's best-loved classics, and you tap a card to see the recipe. A switch shows mocktails, which work the same way.

- **Add favourites.** Save the drinks you love, and they are remembered for next time.
- **Say how many servings.** Quantities are set in servings, in steps of 20, and your bartender can talk the numbers through with you.
- **Recipes on your invoice.** The invoice lists each cocktail with its full recipe scaled to your servings, so your professionals see what you expect.
- **Tips and requests.** Add anything special on the request box. It appears on your Event Card and invoice.
- **Rebook the same drinks.** Your choices stay with you, so booking another party can start from the same cocktails.

Ask the bartender to confirm what they can make before the event.

how-to-plan-a-wedding-bar.title: How to plan a wedding bar
how-to-plan-a-wedding-bar.seo: How to plan a wedding bar: timings, supplies and service
how-to-plan-a-wedding-bar.alt: Vooshka event bar photo: An elegant centrepiece.
how-to-plan-a-wedding-bar.blurb: Plan the wedding bar around your timetable: what is served on arrival, with the meal, and in the evening. Then decide who provides the drinks, the bar and the staff, and check what your...
how-to-plan-a-wedding-bar.intro: Plan the wedding bar around your timetable: what is served on arrival, with the meal, and in the evening. Then decide who provides the drinks, the bar and the staff, and check what your venue allows. Wedding bars are a good place for an experienced team, because the service has to run to time.
body: Build a timetable

| Moment | What the bar usually does |
|---|---|
| Arrival drinks | Short, quick serve: a welcome drink and an alcohol-free option |
| Meal | Table service or wine, with the bar quiet |
| Toasts | Drinks ready for everyone at the same time |
| Evening | Full bar service, often the busiest period |
Venue first

Ask your venue about corkage, whether you can bring your own drinks, who must hold the licence, and what space and power the bar can use. A temporary event notice may be needed where the venue does not already have a licence. Check current guidance for your area.
Decide who runs each part

- **Venue bar.** Simple, but you pay the venue's prices.
- **Bartender with your drinks.** You supply drinks; see [supplying your own alcohol](/stories/supply-own-alcohol-hire-bartender).
- **Bar company.** Stock, glassware, ice and a bar are provided, and a team runs the whole evening. We usually recommend this for 100 guests or more.
Staffing
For 30 to 100 guests, an experienced bartender plus support. For 100 or more, a team. See [how many bartenders you need](/stories/how-many-bartenders-do-i-need).
Paying for drinks
Decide between an open bar, a limited open bar, or a cash bar. See [cash bar or open bar for a wedding](/stories/cash-bar-or-open-bar-for-a-wedding).
Booking

Tell us your date, venue and numbers. The FireFlair team has global events industry experience and can contact bar companies for you. Book early for popular dates: [how far in advance to book](/stories/how-far-in-advance-to-book-a-bartender).

supply-own-alcohol-hire-bartender.title: Can I supply my own alcohol when hiring a bartender?
supply-own-alcohol-hire-bartender.seo: Can I supply my own alcohol when hiring a bartender?
supply-own-alcohol-hire-bartender.blurb: Often yes, but agree it with both your supplier and your venue first. Some suppliers offer a bartender-only service for this, while others price a package that includes drinks.
supply-own-alcohol-hire-bartender.intro: Often yes, but agree it with both your supplier and your venue first. Some suppliers offer a bartender-only service for this, while others price a package that includes drinks.
body: Check three things

1. **Your supplier.** Do they work with client-supplied drinks, and do they want a list?
2. **Your venue.** Some venues do not allow it, or charge corkage.
3. **Licensing.** Check what applies to your event. Temporary event notice rules apply in England and Wales, and other parts of the UK differ.
Planning your stock

- Ask your bartender what to buy for your menu. See [how many cocktails to plan](/stories/how-many-cocktails-for-a-party).
- Plan mixers, ice, garnishes and glassware too.
- Store drinks cold and out of the way, and agree where the bartender will find them.
Leftovers
Decide in advance who keeps unopened bottles.
The trade-off

Buying your own can save effort in some cases and cost in others. A package that includes drinks is simpler, with one price and one supplier. See [bartender hire vs mobile bar hire](/stories/bartender-hire-vs-mobile-bar-hire).

what-to-ask-before-booking-a-bartender.title: What to Ask Before Booking a Bartender for a Private Party
what-to-ask-before-booking-a-bartender.seo: What to ask before booking a bartender
what-to-ask-before-booking-a-bartender.alt: A smiling bartender in black leans on the bar behind a tall creamy pink cocktail with a mint and pineapple garnish.
what-to-ask-before-booking-a-bartender.blurb: The questions to ask about experience, drinks, equipment and service before booking a bartender for a private party.
what-to-ask-before-booking-a-bartender.intro: Before booking a bartender, ask about experience with your kind of party, what the service includes, and how your booking is confirmed. A bartender at a birthday might serve a signature cocktail as guests arrive and keep the bar running through the evening. At a masterclass, the same professional might spend their time guiding guests through the drinks. Tell the person you're considering what you want your guests to experience. Their answers will help you choose someone who suits the occasion.
body: Have you worked on a party like mine?

Share the occasion, guest numbers, location, and the hours you'd like drinks served. Look at examples of their work and any relevant reviews. Ask how they'd handle arrivals if most guests come at once, and what sort of menu they'd suggest for your space and timings.
What will each of us provide?

Ask who brings ingredients, ice, glassware, tools, and a bar setup. Check how much setup space they need and whether setup and clear-down are included in the agreed hours or price. If you already have a favourite drink in mind, check whether they can serve it and offer an alcohol-free option alongside it. For a full checklist, see [what to provide when you hire a bartender](/stories/what-to-provide-when-hiring-a-bartender).
What will the booking cover?

Before you commit, review the service, hours, inclusions, and total cost. Check what you need to pay, when the booking becomes confirmed, and how to contact the professional if the plan changes. A short written brief with the agreed details gives you both something to refer back to before the event.

when-to-serve-cocktails-at-a-party.title: Welcome Drinks, a Cocktail Hour or a Bar All Evening?
when-to-serve-cocktails-at-a-party.seo: Welcome drinks, a cocktail hour or a bar all evening?
when-to-serve-cocktails-at-a-party.alt: A single foamy martini with rose petals, lit warmly on a wooden table.
when-to-serve-cocktails-at-a-party.blurb: Pick the format that matches how your guests arrive and how long you want the bar to run.
when-to-serve-cocktails-at-a-party.intro: Choose welcome drinks if you want a lively start, a cocktail hour if you want one special moment, and a bar all evening if cocktails are part of the whole party. Each works well. The right one depends on how your guests arrive and how long you want the bar open.
body: The three formats

| Format | Suits | When the first round goes out | Menu length | Tell your bartender |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Welcome drinks | Dinner or a seated meal to follow | As guests arrive | One or two signature drinks | Arrival window and when drinks finish |
| Cocktail hour | A barbecue, birthday or celebration with a focus moment | At the start of the defined window | A short menu guests can choose from | The window and the main moment, such as a toast |
| Bar all evening | Hosts who want cocktails throughout | When the first guests arrive | A fuller menu | Start, finish and any quiet points |
Welcome drinks before dinner

Arrival drinks give guests something in hand while others come in. They work best when most people arrive close together. A signature welcome drink keeps service quick, so the bartender can greet people rather than answer long menu questions.
A defined cocktail window

A window suits a barbecue or a birthday, where food and conversation share the evening. In my own work with house parties, a lot of the events I look after are barbecues, and a set window helps the bartender plan prep and keep the quality high. Choose the start and the end, then make a short menu for guests to pick from.
A bar for the whole evening

If you want cocktails from arrival to the last song, tell the bartender the full time. A longer service suits a wider menu and a slower pace. Typical shifts in my examples run two to four hours, so a longer evening is worth planning early.
Plan around your guests

- Guests arriving around one time: a first-round welcome drink lands well.
- Guests arriving across a longer window: a bar open for longer, or a window in the middle of the party.
- A larger event: one mixologist can serve a particular group or time window.

These examples are flexible. Start with the one that fits, then adjust.
What to put in the brief

Share the start time, the finish, the guest numbers and how they will arrive, the menu, and who will meet the bartender. Read [how to hire a bartender for a house party](/stories/how-to-hire-a-bartender-for-a-house-party), [how many bartenders you need](/stories/how-many-bartenders-do-i-need) and [how to plan a cocktail menu for a party](/stories/how-to-plan-a-cocktail-menu-for-a-party), then browse FireFlair Packages to match your format.

body: Three models

| Model | You pay | Risk |
|---|---|---|
| **Pay for leads** | For each enquiry or lead credit | You pay whether or not you win the job |
| **Commission** | A share of confirmed bookings | Cost rises with larger bookings |

Measure lead quality

For any source, track:

1. Enquiries received
2. Enquiries that fit your service and area
3. Quotes sent
4. Bookings confirmed
5. Cost per confirmed booking

A cheap lead that never books costs more than a dearer one that does.

bar-staffing-agency-or-freelance-platfor.intro: A managed agency usually supplies and manages the staff for you. A freelance platform lets you choose from individual professionals. FireFlair connects you with professionals and handles the booking, and the pay and working arrangement are agreed between you and each professional. Your choice depends on how much choosing, managing and responsibility you want.
body: What differs

| | Managed agency | Freelance platform |
|---|---|---|
| **Who selects** | The agency, to your brief | You, from profiles, or the platform matches |
| **Support** | Often a named account contact and cover | Varies by platform |
| **Payroll and pay** | Often handled by the agency | Varies; some platforms handle payment, others leave it to you |
| **Cost shape** | May be an hourly client rate | May be a percentage fee, or a fixed fee per booking |
| **Responsibility** | Depends on the arrangement | Depends on the arrangement |

Employment status and liability depend on the actual working arrangement, not on what a contract calls it. Check current Acas and government guidance, or take advice, before you rely on any one model.
When an agency may fit

- You need a large team or multiple events at once.
- You want a single contact who takes responsibility for supply.
- You want payroll and compliance handled for you.

Examples include general hospitality agencies and bar specialists such as Off to Work, Wilde Toast, Viking Staffing & Events and Flair.
When a platform may fit

- You want to see and choose individuals.
- You want to rebook the same people.
- You want costs that are clear up front.

barback-bartender-or-bar-manager.blurb: A bartender makes and serves drinks, a barback keeps the bar stocked and clean, and a bar manager runs the bar and its team. The right mix depends on the size and style of the event.
barback-bartender-or-bar-manager.intro: A bartender makes and serves drinks, a barback keeps the bar stocked and clean, and a bar manager runs the bar and its team. The right mix depends on the size and style of the event.
body: Responsibilities

| Role | Typical responsibilities |
|---|---|
| **Barback** | Ice, glassware, restocking, clearing, keeping the bar clean |
| **Bartender** | Taking orders, making and serving drinks, handling payment where relevant |
| **Bar manager** | Planning the bar, stock, team, timings and problem-solving |

Agencies such as Off to Work and Wilde Toast Events advertise these roles, among others.
Scenarios

- **Small private party:** one experienced bartender may be enough.
- **Mid-sized event:** a bartender plus support.
- **Large reception:** several bartenders, one or more barbacks and a lead.
A lead is not always a manager
Naming someone as the contact on the day is different from paying someone to manage. If you want management duties, say so in the brief and agree the pay for them.
Booking
Request each role on its own Shift Card where the pay or requirements differ. See [staffing a launch or drinks reception](/stories/staffing-a-product-launch-or-drinks-reception).

bartender-decisions-company-booking.title: What Should a Bartender Be Able to Decide on a Company Booking?
bartender-decisions-company-booking.seo: What should a bartender decide on a company booking?
bartender-decisions-company-booking.alt: Close-up of layered white and red shots, softly out of focus.
bartender-decisions-company-booking.blurb: Agree who can say yes on the night, and who needs to approve a change, before the booking starts.
bartender-decisions-company-booking.intro: A bartender can decide how service runs inside the agreed brief. Anything that changes the price, the hours or a signature recipe goes back to the company first. Agreeing that split before the booking keeps the night smooth.
body: Three kinds of decision

- **Service on the night.** Timing of rounds, order of service and how the bar is set out, all within the agreed hours.
- **Choices from an approved list.** A menu option the company has already said can be offered.
- **Changes that need the company.** Price, hours, extra stock, glassware or bar hire, and anything that alters a signature recipe.

A signature recipe belongs to the company that created it. The company decides what is shared with the bartender and with the host.
A worked scenario

This scenario is illustrative. A host books a bar company for an evening and knows the company's signature cocktail. On the day they ask about an ingredient swap, extra glassware and a later finish.

| The host asks | Who decides | Where it is recorded |
|---|---|---|
| An ingredient swap in the signature cocktail | The company, since the recipe is theirs | The booking notes, once approved |
| Extra glassware | The company, because it affects stock and cost | The booking notes and the updated quote |
| A later finish | The company, because it changes hours | The booking notes and the updated hours |
| Running the first round when guests arrive | The bartender, within the agreed hours | Nothing further needed |
Let the host and bartender talk

Alex Gagnon, founder of FireFlair, takes the view that it works best when the bartender and the client communicate directly about the brief. The approvals above sit alongside that. The bartender answers questions about the evening, and the company keeps control of recipe, price and hours.
Write it into the brief

Name an approver in the brief, so the bartender knows who to contact when a request falls outside the agreement. Add a line for changes: who agreed them and what the final arrangement is. Most items from the [brief template](/stories/temporary-bar-staff-brief-template) go into the fields of a Shift Card, and anything extra goes into the notes.

For team planning, see [how to rebook bartenders and build a regular event team](/stories/how-to-rebook-bartenders) and [what to do when an event bartender cancels](/stories/what-to-do-when-an-event-bartender-cancels).

ff-staff-booking-fees-refunds-replacemen.intro: FF Staff has one fee for businesses: a £10 booking connection fee for each Shift Card that is filled. It is taken when you send the card and refunded if the card cannot be filled. It is not £10 per person and not £10 per hour, so a one-hour shift and a ten-hour shift carry the same fee. The professional's pay is separate and agreed with them. Check the current booking terms for the exact conditions.
body: What you pay

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| FireFlair booking connection fee | £10 for each filled Shift Card |
| Professional's pay | Agreed with each professional and shown separately |
| Autofill | No extra fee |

A Shift Card with several positions carries one fee. Separate Shift Cards for different roles carry a fee each.
If a Shift Card is not filled

The booking connection fee is taken before your Shift Card is sent out, so that the request goes to professionals. If the card cannot be filled, the fee is refunded. Before you confirm anyone you can also choose Cancel request, and the fee is refunded.
Several cards and part-filled cards

Each Shift Card is treated separately. You keep the fee only for the cards that are filled. A card that asks for several people where only some are found is reviewed individually. There is no published per-person formula.
After you and the professional have both confirmed
If you cancel after both of you have confirmed, the booking connection fee is not refunded. Any pay or cancellation payment owed to the professional is agreed between you and them.
Replacements
If a confirmed professional cancels, the position is reopened and a replacement is sought through the agreed process, with no further replacement-matching fee. A replacement depends on availability.
The record

The website is the official record. WhatsApp and email carry notifications.

hospitality-staffing-fees-explained.intro: Staffing is paid for in four common ways: a fixed fee per booking, an hourly mark-up, a percentage of the booking and a subscription. Compare them on the same event, and keep the fee separate from the worker's pay and from payroll costs.
body: The structures

| Structure | How it works | Moves with |
|---|---|---|
| **Fixed per booking** | One amount for each booking | Number of bookings |
| **Hourly** | A rate for every hour worked | Length of the shift |
| **Percentage** | A share of the booking value | Size of the booking |
| **Subscription** | A regular payment for access | Time, not use |
A matched example (fictional)

Take a 6-hour shift with a worker paid £20 an hour, so £120 in pay.

- **Hourly agency charging £40 an hour:** £240 for the shift.
- **Fixed booking fee, as on FF Staff:** £120 pay plus a £10 booking connection fee, so £130.
- **Percentage service:** a 10% fee on £120 is £12, plus any payroll costs it adds.

Make the shift 10 hours and the hourly cost rises, while the fixed fee stays at £10. The figures are examples, not quotes from any company. Check what each service charges and who pays.
Keep these separate

- **Fee:** what the service charges.
- **Pay:** what the worker earns.
- **Payroll and employment costs:** who handles tax, National Insurance and holiday pay depends on the arrangement.

how-to-book-bar-staff-on-ff-staff.intro: You create an event, add a shift for each role, then invite people by name or let Autofill find them. FireFlair's booking connection fee of £10 applies to each Shift Card that is filled. Someone is booked only when they accept and confirm, or when you choose a professional who has said they are available.
body: How the pieces fit

An Event Card holds your event. Each role you need is a Shift Card, and a Shift Card can ask for several professionals. Each position and each invitation is tracked separately. The minimum you need is a phone number, an email, the event and shift details, payment and acceptance of the terms. You do not need a company account first.
A worked example (fictional)

*A hotel needs a drinks reception on Friday 6pm to 11pm: three bartenders and one barback.*

1. Create the Event Card with the date, place and timings.
2. Add a Shift Card for bartenders and ask for three positions. Add a second Shift Card for the barback, which has a different role and pay.
3. Add duties, hours, pay, dress code and requirements.
4. The booking connection fee is £10 for each Shift Card that is filled, so the two cards here would carry £20 in total. The pay for each professional is separate and agreed with them.
5. Choose people from the staff row, or choose Autofill.
Choose a person, or Autofill

**By name.** The person is invited exclusively for up to 24 hours, never beyond the shift start. If they choose Accept & confirm, the position is filled with no second approval.

**Autofill.** It invites professionals who match the role and work near you, normally ten at a time. Their reply "Available" is not a booking: you see who is available and any questions, then choose. Discuss first confirms nothing and does not extend a deadline.
How long you have to choose
Each invitation has its own deadline, normally the earlier of seven days after it was created and the shift start. A reply does not restart the seven days. Your booking page shows the real deadline.
After confirmation

You receive the booking reference, shift details, profile link and contact details. The website is the official record, and WhatsApp and email carry notifications. See [fees, refunds and replacements](/stories/ff-staff-booking-fees-refunds-replacements) for what happens if something changes.

body: Write the brief in five lines

1. Date, start and finish, and exact address.
2. Role and how many people.
3. Must-have skills, for example solo bar or classic cocktails.
4. Pay for the shift.
5. Who they meet and what they wear.

A complete brief gets faster answers because professionals do not need to ask. See [how to write a brief for temporary bar staff](/stories/temporary-bar-staff-brief-template).
Be realistic about timing

Professionals have up to 24 hours to reply to an invitation, and never beyond the shift start. That is a response window. It does not guarantee a reply or a confirmed booking within a day. For urgent shifts:

- Invite several matching professionals rather than waiting on one.
- Use Autofill alongside people you already know.
- Keep a backup plan until someone is confirmed.

Each invitation shows its real deadline, normally the earlier of seven days after creation and the shift start.
Check it is confirmed
"Available" is not a booking. You are covered only when a professional has accepted and confirmed, or when you have chosen them. Check your booking page, which is the official record.
If you cannot fill it

If nobody is confirmed, the unfilled Shift Card is refunded under the policy. See [fees, refunds and replacements](/stories/ff-staff-booking-fees-refunds-replacements). If someone cancels, see [what to do when an event bartender cancels](/stories/what-to-do-when-an-event-bartender-cancels).

small-cocktail-event-profitability.intro: Yes, when the quote covers the work around the two hours as well as the drinks. A short booking is rarely a short job, so the answer comes from counting everything that happens before service.
body: Where the time goes

Alex Gagnon, founder of FireFlair, once ran a team of ten bartenders and found most of his own time went on messaging them. That is one practitioner's experience, and it points at a cost that is easy to leave out of a quote.

Before a bartender pours a drink, someone has usually:

1. Qualified the enquiry and confirmed the date, place and guest numbers.
2. Found the right person.
3. Settled the menu with the host.
4. Assigned stock and equipment.
5. Confirmed travel and arrival.
6. Sent the brief.
A worksheet to fill in

This worksheet is illustrative. It has no figures because every business counts differently. Fill each line in from your own records.

| Line | What to include | Where the number comes from |
|---|---|---|
| Quote | What the host pays for the booking | Your agreed quote |
| Direct costs | Staff time on the night, stock, ice, glassware, consumables, travel | Your supplier and staff records |
| Contribution | Quote minus direct costs | The two lines above |
| Admin time | Quoting, matching, menu, brief, follow-up | A simple time log for the next five bookings |
| Value of admin time | Admin time at the rate you would pay for the work | Your own rate |
| Result | Contribution minus value of admin time | The lines above |

Run the worksheet on three recent small bookings. The pattern across them tells you more than any single job.
Standardise or quote bespoke?

| Element | Often suits a standard approach | Often needs a bespoke quote |
|---|---|---|
| Menu | A set menu with defined inclusions | A new menu built around the host's recipe |
| Staffing | A fixed bartender-to-guest pattern | Unusual venue, access or hours |
| Equipment | A standard kit list | Specialist equipment or bar hire |
| Brief | One template for every booking | Details only this host has |

Standardising a part of the job means fewer messages and quicker quotes. Keep bespoke quotes for the parts where the host wants something different.
Where FF Staff fits

A complete [brief](/stories/temporary-bar-staff-brief-template) does much of the coordination in one go: most of its items go into the fields of a Shift Card, so the person who accepts the shift sees what you need. body: The cost components

- **Pay** for the shift, including setup and clear-down if you agree them.
- **Hours**, because pay and many fees grow with time.
- **Booking fee or agency charge**, and how it is calculated.
- **Employer costs or payroll**, depending on the arrangement.

How providers charge

Most agencies charge by the hour: the worker is paid one rate and the client is billed a higher one. For example (invented, to show the arithmetic), if a bartender is paid £20 an hour and the agency bills you £40 an hour, a 10-hour shift costs you £400 while the bartender receives £200. The difference pays for the agency's costs, which can include payroll, insurance and administration, so it is not all profit. Percentage models work similarly: Brigad's pages describe a percentage service fee, and limber's pricing page describes a percentage fee with wages and employment costs additional.

FF Staff charges a fixed £10 booking connection fee for each Shift Card that is filled. It is not per person and not per hour, so a one-hour shift and a ten-hour shift carry the same fee, and the professional's pay is agreed with them. The same bartender at £20 an hour for 10 hours costs £200 in pay plus the £10 fee, which is £210. This is first-year launch pricing, which FireFlair has said will stay fixed for loyal users.

| Three bartenders and one barback on two Shift Cards (barback at £15 an hour for 5 hours) | £375 | £20 | £395 |

The government has announced it will increase to £3,000 from 6 April 2027, subject to the legislation. body: The current rule

If your gross self-employed income from your trade is £1,000 or less in a tax year, you can use the trading allowance and generally do not need to report it. If it is more, you normally need to register for Self Assessment, and the usual deadline is 5 October after the end of the tax year. Check the current guidance on gov.uk.
What is changing

HMRC published a policy paper on 28 October 2026. It describes increasing the trading allowance from £1,000 to £3,000 from 6 April 2027, for the 2027 to 2028 tax year onwards, and raising the Self Assessment reporting threshold to the same level. The measure is due to be legislated in the Finance Bill 2026-27, so check that it has been enacted before you rely on it.

Until 6 April 2027, nothing has changed.
What counts

The allowance applies to your gross income from your own trade, before costs. It covers everything you do on your own account, not each job separately. It does not apply to pay from an employer taxed through PAYE.
Choose the allowance or your expenses
If your real costs are higher than the allowance, you may be better off deducting actual expenses instead. You cannot do both.
Keep records
Whatever you do, keep a record of what you earn. On FF Team, your Bookings page lists your shifts, which helps you add up a year's work. FireFlair does not take tax from your pay.
Sources
HMRC, "Increasing the trading allowance", policy paper published 28 October 2026. GOV.UK guidance on tax-free allowances on property and trading income. Check both before relying on this page.

body: Read the card first

The card shows what you need to decide: role, duties, location, date, hours, pay, dress code, requirements and terms. Requests arrive on WhatsApp and on your Bookings page. The website is the official record.
Two kinds of invitation

| | Invited by name (exclusive) | Autofill |
|---|---|---|
| Who gets it | You alone | A batch of matching professionals, normally ten |
| Your time to reply | Up to 24 hours, never beyond the shift start | Up to 24 hours |
| Accept & confirm | You are booked straight away, with no second approval | Not available |
| Available | Not needed | You tell the booker you can do it. You are **not** booked until they choose you |
| Discuss first | Ask a question. It does not confirm anything | Same. It does not extend any deadline |
| Decline | Frees the booker to invite someone else | Same |

Up to 24 hours is the time you have to reply. It is not a promise from FireFlair to answer you or confirm a booking within a day.
Ask before you commit
Use Discuss first to check things such as transport, duties or whether pay can change. Only a person at FireFlair can change the pay or terms shown on the card.
When you are confirmed
You and the booker receive the booking reference, shift details, profile links and the supported contact details. Your contact details are shared only once you are confirmed.
If you cannot make it
Open the booking and choose Cancel shift. FireFlair is told straight away and works to find a replacement. Cancel as early as you can, because the booker is relying on you.
After the event

Leave and receive reviews on the website. They become part of your profile and help you get booked again.

body: The structure that works

1. **A clear photo.** Bright, friendly, ideally you at work. Keep your face and head fully in frame.
2. **Your professions.** Use the titles people type: cocktail bartender, flair bartender, mixologist, bar manager, barback. See [the difference between a bartender, mixologist and flair bartender](/stories/bartender-mixologist-flair-bartender-difference).
3. **Where you work.** Add the areas you cover. Your Profile Card appears by area, never by your address.
4. **Evidence of skill.** Name what you can make and run: a classic menu, high-volume service, event setup, solo bars. Be specific and be honest.
5. **Reviews.** Ask the person who booked you to leave one after the event. A few good reviews do more than any description.
6. **Your people.** Add colleagues you have worked with. A connection means you know each other; it does not prove you worked a particular event together.
Example (fictional)

> **Sam R.** Cocktail bartender · Hertfordshire and north London
> Eight years in hotel and event bars. Classic cocktail menus, solo bar setup for up to 60 guests, alcohol-free menus. Travels with own tools. Can bring a barback by arrangement.

This is an invented example to show the level of detail. Do not copy it. Use your own facts.
Mistakes to avoid

- Claiming experience you cannot back up.
- Using a photo that hides your face or is cropped badly.
- Listing every possible role. A focused profile is easier to book.

Your public profile also works alongside a CV. See [how to write a bartender CV](/stories/how-to-write-a-bartender-cv).

body: The five routes

| Route | How it works | Worth knowing |
|---|---|---|
| **Work platforms** | You join, set your availability and accept shifts. Examples include Indeed Flex (a dedicated bartender route), Brigad and Stint. | Check what each takes from your pay or charges the business, and what commitment it asks for. |

| **Event bar companies** | Companies that run bars at weddings, parties and corporate events book freelancers for busy dates. | Contact them directly and ask what they look for. |
| **Referrals** | Other bartenders, managers and past clients pass work on. | The strongest route. See [repeat bookings](/stories/repeat-bookings-freelance-bartender). |
| **Direct to venues** | You approach bars, hotels and venues for cover shifts. | Slower, and works best when you already know someone. |

What makes you bookable

- A clear profile with the roles you do, the areas you cover and honest photos. See [how to build a bartender profile](/stories/how-to-build-a-bartender-profile).
- Reviews and people who will vouch for you.
- Fast replies. A booking request often goes to the first person who answers.
- Clear terms before you accept. Use the [shift checklist](/stories/what-to-check-before-accepting-a-bar-shift).
Where FF Team fits

FF Team starts with bartenders. You build a Profile Card that shows your craft, experience, work areas and the people you work with, and you can share it by link. Event hosts and businesses invite you to shifts, and you see the details before you commit. A free profile has no percentage taken from your agreed pay, and the booking fee is paid by the person booking, not by you.

The pay for each type of booking is listed up front. In the prototype, a bartending shift of 3 hours pays £100, a cocktail (mixology) shift from 4 hours pays £150, and a flair performance from 2 hours pays £200. If you sign up, you can talk directly with the client before the event.

last-minute-bartending-shifts.intro: The phone would ring, an agency would tell me where they needed me, and I would go. That simple routine shaped most of my early career.
body: Five agencies in London

I spent a few years in London working for around five different agencies. Each one had its own clients, so the work kept changing. One week I might be behind a hotel bar; the next, at a party where everything about the night had been planned with care.

Some of those calls sent me to five-star hotels and to the best parties I had worked. Saying yes to a short-notice booking meant meeting new teams, seeing how different venues ran their service and learning quickly. A bartender who can walk into a room, read it and settle in is a bartender people ask for again.
What the work paid for

The agency shifts gave me the means to travel. I used the money to visit some of the best cocktail bars around the world. I watched how they welcomed guests, built their menus and trained their teams. That time away taught me that hospitality can open far more doors than most people expect from a night behind a bar.
What I would keep

Looking back, three things made those short-notice shifts worth taking:

- A clear picture of the job before I accepted it: place, hours and what was expected.
- A team I could learn from on the night.
- A way for the next person to find me, which is where I was short for years.

That last point matters most. Every job I did well stayed in the memory of the people who were there. Almost none of it was visible to anyone who had not been in the room.
Why I want FF Team to help

My focus today is on creating opportunities for other people. FF Team gives bartenders and other hospitality professionals a Profile Card that shows who they are, what they do well and who they work with, so good work can be found again.

If you are building your own freelance career, start with [a profile that gets booked](/stories/how-to-build-a-bartender-profile), then grow [your network of people you would work with again](/stories/how-to-build-a-bartender-network).

What people wanted to find

Asked about hard-to-find events they would be interested in attending, 40% picked pop-up experiences or installations and 36% picked speakeasies or underground bars. Source: [Eventbrite Social Study 2026, p. 6](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260114088488/en).

body: The checklist

| Check | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Duties** | Bar service only, or also barback work, stock, glass collection or setup? |
| **Total hours** | Do paid hours include setup and finish, or only service? |
| **Arrival time and place** | Access, parking, loading, who meets you |
| **Rate and who pays** | Is the pay per hour or for the shift? Who pays, you from the booker or an agency? |
| **Payment date and method** | When, how, and whether you invoice |
| **Breaks** | When and how long |
| **Uniform and kit** | What you wear and what you bring |
| **Menu** | Cocktail list or simple service? Can you learn it in time? |
| **Support** | Is there a barback or manager? Who is your contact on the night? |
| **Transport home** | Late finishes, last trains, paid taxi |
| **Cancellation** | What happens if the event is cancelled or you cannot attend |
Two sample briefs (fictional)

**Brief A: house party.** Saturday 7pm to midnight, home in Hertford, 40 guests, five classic cocktails supplied by host, 30 minutes setup, bring your own tools. Pay for the whole shift, paid by the host. *Questions to ask: is setup paid, who supplies ice and glassware, how do I get home?*

**Brief B: corporate drinks reception.** Thursday 6pm to 10pm, two bartenders and a barback, 120 guests, wine, beer and one signature drink, uniform provided, contact is the venue manager. Agency pays on the 15th of the following month. *Questions to ask: what is the rate, are breaks covered, what if the event ends early?*

On FF Team the card shows most of these. Use Discuss first for anything missing. See [how to accept bookings on FF Team](/stories/how-to-accept-bookings-on-ff-team).

body: What a colleague can tell you

A person who worked a shift next to you can speak to things a CV cannot show:

- How quickly someone prepared before service.
- Their pace when the bar was three deep.
- How they handed over at the end of the night.
- How they worked with the rest of the team.

Those are specific, checkable observations. They carry weight because they come from someone who was there.
Three different things

It helps to keep three ideas apart:

- **A connection** means two people know each other. It does not show that you worked a particular event together.
- **A recommendation** is a colleague saying what they saw you do, from real work.
- **A check** is a separate step that confirms something factual, such as an identity or a qualification.

On FF Team, you can add people you have worked with to your profile, and the people who book you can see who you work alongside. Alex Gagnon, founder of FireFlair, has described community verification as one of the core ideas behind FF Team: the people who know your work are the best witnesses to it.
If you are new

Everyone starts with no relationships in the trade. The quickest way to build them:

1. Work events with the same team when you can.
2. After a shift, ask the person who led it what they noticed about your work.
3. Add the people you worked with, and recommend them in return.

A first recommendation can be as simple as a lead saying you arrived prepared and stayed calm under pressure.
Put it on your profile

Your Profile Card is the place where the people you worked with, the skills you are known for and the areas you cover come together. Share it with a colleague and they can see in one view who you are as a professional.

For more on building a trusted crew, read [how to build a bartender network and work with a team](/stories/how-to-build-a-bartender-network) and [how to get repeat bookings as a freelance bartender](/stories/repeat-bookings-freelance-bartender).
